elements.quote: The use of Point-of-care ultrasound (PoCUS) has gained increasing popularity in several domains of acute patient management, including acute onset dyspnea [11, 15]. There is an increasing body of evidence demonstrating that the accuracy of PoCUS is comparable to the current imaging reference standard CXR in general [16] as well as in specific conditions, such as pneumonia [17], acute decompensated heart failure [16], pleural effusion [18], pneumothorax [19] and pulmonary embolism [20]. PoCUS has other advantages, such as being free from ionizing radiation, and most importantly can be performed in real-time at the bedside [16, 21]. Additionally, PoCUS can answer a broad spectrum of remaining diagnostic questions and may also help to optimize and personalize therapy [22]. However, very few trials have examined meaningful clinical outcomes related to PoCUS usage to date [23] and the results on outcome measurements were heterogeneous [24].
elements.reason: Describes existing evidence on PoCUS accuracy/advantages and highlights uncertainties/knowledge gaps regarding clinical outcomes and heterogeneity.

elements.quote: Therefore, rapid and appropriate diagnosis of the underlying pathology is of utmost importance for prompt and adequate treatment [9]. However, differential diagnosis is often challenging [10, 11]. Most physicians mainly rely on conventional diagnostic modalities, such as medical history, physical examination, chest X-ray (CXR), electrocardiogram (ECG), and standard laboratory tests [12]. Even given all these tests, some studies have raised doubts about the diagnostic accuracy of these conventional approaches, especially in the critically ill patient population [13, 14]. Therefore, we conducted a high-quality, comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis that included the most recent publications that reported clinical outcomes with the use of PoCUS in patients who developed acute onset dyspnea.
elements.reason: Explains why a review is needed: acute-onset dyspnea diagnosis is important but challenging, conventional modalities may have diagnostic accuracy doubts, and PoCUS clinical outcome evidence requires synthesis.

elements.quote: In contrast to previous reviews and meta-analyses [16-20, 60] that analyzed data from patients with an explicit diagnosis, such as pneumonia or acute decompensated heart failure [9, 10, 16, 17, 62], we applied a broader definition of dyspnea, thereby including more patients and providing more comprehensive results.
elements.reason: Identifies prior reviews/meta-analyses and explains the need for the current review by stating it differs through a broader dyspnea definition and includes more patients.
No explicit description of a proposed mechanism of action of PoCUS (for intervention effects) is provided in the retrieved evidence.
No logic model or hypothesised relationships between PoCUS components and outcomes are presented in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: In addition to the existing diagnostic accuracy studies [16-20, 25], our main objective, as a new insight to this field, was to investigate how PoCUS improves clinical endpoints in patients with acute onset dyspnea.
elements.reason: The review objective is explicitly stated (“main objective… was to investigate how PoCUS improves clinical endpoints…”), but it is not clearly expressed in a relevant question-formulation framework (e.g., explicitly structured question).

elements.quote: The selected studies had to match our previously defined PICO (Patients, Intervention, Control, Outcome) framework: ... P: Adults and children ... eligible. ... I: The examined intervention was PoCUS use on its own or in combination with conventional diagnostic measures. ... C: Control group included conventional diagnostic methods, such as taking the patients' medical history, physical examination, ECG, blood gas and different laboratory analyses, echocardiography, CXR, or computer tomography (CT).
elements.reason: Planned comparisons are stated using an explicit PICO framework, including the intervention (PoCUS) and control (conventional diagnostic methods), for eligible patients.

elements.quote: The selected studies had to match our previously defined PICO (Patients, Intervention, Control, Outcome) framework: ... P: Adults and children who were admitted to the ED or to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU), or to another inpatient setting because of acute onset or worsening dyspnea were eligible. ... Studies reporting on trauma-induced acute onset dyspnea, or pregnancy were excluded. ... I: The examined intervention was PoCUS use on its own or in combination with conventional diagnostic measures. ... There were no restrictions on the type of PoCUS protocols. ... C: Control group included conventional diagnostic methods, such as taking the patients' medical history, physical examination, ECG, blood gas and different laboratory analyses, echocardiography, CXR, or computer tomography (CT).
elements.reason: Eligibility is described using the PICO framework, including participants, intervention, and control, and some exclusions are stated. However, the evidence does not specify all study-characteristic components required (e.g., eligible study designs/settings are partially described, and follow-up requirements are not reported here).

elements.quote: We did not use any restrictions or limitations based on language or publication date.

elements.quote: Heterogeneity among these trials for both outcomes was considerable ( I 2 = 100%, p = 0 and 88%, p < 0.01, respectively). ... elements.quote: To estimate the heterogeneity variance measure, τ 2 was applied estimated with the Q profile method.

elements.quote: If the study number for the given outcome was over five, the Hartung-Knapp adjustment [30, 31] was applied. If the mean and SD were not reported in the article, we estimated them from the medians, quartiles, minimum and maximums using the Luo [32] and Shi [33] methods. ... Due to the low number of available studies, the Egger's test for the small-study effect could not be performed.
elements.reason: Provides additional random-effects implementation details (Hartung-Knapp adjustment criteria, raw data rules, imputation approach for mean/SD, and notes on Egger’s test feasibility).
